items.text: It's a great review. I agree with Miss Y about the fact that even people who love the Cirque shows might not enjoy this one specifically. Different subject really though. For me it's best the theatre and visual design. The scenery and decor is really stunning, start to finish. The idea and concept is beautiful, really appeals to me. But for some reason it doesn't really translate very well to live performance. Storyline really not too fun. And when we went to see one performance the stage malfunctions throughout the whole evening making it difficult to really stay focused even in good scenes. Le Reve tries to have the Cirque flair and spectacle just doesn't quite achieve it. So go see it mostly to see what great theatre experience, otherwise save your money for the other shows.

Paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard on the cheap. I reckon I got about $38 worth of keyboard, a little more, not more really. The space bar rattles for some odd reason. Every hit is hollow with clack clacking like shaking up cutlery from a tray. My mind goes to it but I tune it out during the day. I type around it at midnight sometimes. It doesn't bother me as much because I don't see it as a rattle. But I can get so annoyed. Like I can be typing words, the 'E' button is repeat sometimes. And it's so rare but frequent enough I read my emails and text messages over and over to make sure I'm writing what I want to. It's every third paragraph. Messaged the seller, asked, got bored and it came a week later, a few days after I got the keyboard. Brown switches for the record. I'm keeping it cause the comfort is nice. There's a stop at half down in every button that tells me I pressed it without slamming into the full bottom. So my fingers can do long emails and after it's not too tired or sore like typing on that laptop keyboard. Considered sending it back but that would have cost a lot out of the 38. And it puts me back on the laptop so not worth the shipping fee. And it remains the rattle and all.

Saw this show in Vegas recently and I do recommend it but took off a star for me. Storyline kinda hard to follow at times and a few songs sleepy or not right for the action but performers are incredible. Real impressive athletic ability physiques aerobic skills and females especially impressive, they can stay underwater for minutes. Whole theatre is circular with the stage being circular and each seat gets a really good view. Three main entrances to the stage. Used through-out the production, very prominent at main story transitions. Stage and setting really beautiful overall with lighting, very memorable vibes. Tickets a fair price compared to "O" or "Love". Just wanted more spectacular effects with the fire etc but that is not an issue. I would recommend the show regardless, very entertaining and visually striking.

So remote work sells itself as this one size fits all, but after mentoring five juniors for 2 years, honestly it's a little overblown. They're still in a learning phase.

What they actually need is getting caught up on the design calls or watching the seniors or more senior people debug stuff. They ask questions before they go into that mode where they're confused for a long period of time. That's what it's designed to achieve. And that kind of interaction, I think, in an office it happens naturally organically. But it's not something that can happen remote and it needs them to know when is the right time to cut in, make the call, explain the problem that they might not even fully understand yet. And that's a skill to be able to have it and that's before you even get a chance to learn it.

I've had the problems of feedback. And so comments on a code review is the final word instead of a learning opportunity because you just see short comments. Also, it takes longer, and as a whole, less momentum. Typically, the ones that I had, it improved them faster that they could actually pair up or whiteboard. Or something more organic that you get with the seniors more easily and be in front of people.

I'm not advocating for offices or anti-flexibility. It does work for senior devs and even mid level and even for juniors. It's for self-driven developers. But I think as a whole junior development suffers as you send them off with laptop and calendar. And that will have a lot of downsides. It's a drag on junior development and in turn it'll cause less good technical leadership in the future.

I think there is a typo in the draft, is it meant to be just 'sourdough' not 'sour'. Anyway. At this time the bread should not be baked. Elias was checking door locks and I think it's meant to be the front door? The mixer was still going, and there was flour dust everywhere, like snow, I get why it was left on. 3:17 am, sourdough loaves were in the wooden boards not baked yet so crusts were soft and pale. And then he puts the book back on the glass case where he found it, lining up the spine. After the book, I think he turned off the light. Then there was some notebook paper folded up inside. The message he read was a note. And he stared at it. He then put it back and turned off the light over the glass case, and left it there in shadow. He was staring at his own hands for some time. His hands were reddish, white dusted. He did check the lock on the door. And also he wiped his hands on the apron too, which was all wet and stiff with dough. The book sat there, on the counter or display table for 6 weeks, every Thursday, it just showed up, with no library marks, just was there.

Apple deserves a shoutout. My school only allowed them in middle and high school. But they are double the price for PC's, and the stuff kept breaking all the time. My machine went through 5 hard drives over 4 yrs. The OS was constantly being reinstalled (and I never even dropped my laptop). Worst case was my friend's MacBook Pro catching fire while he was watching a film, smoke alarm going off. Apple support couldn't properly diagnose the issues so they'd just backup then wipe then restore all over again constantly. Same with iPhones, I had one of the first phones and it had so many problems. Now they release a new model like every 2 months. Only the camera is a bit better, barely makes sense. One positive, qualified: iPads are currently the best tablet. But android might catch up some day.

Quick take on the new show, AWAKENING, at Wynn, which is at Wynn Las Vegas: it's good, but not one of those Vegas shows I'd plan a trip around just to see. I've been to Vegas a ton as a kid, saw many shows, before I hit 21, so I have a rough barometer of how these things work. The round stage was a nice feature. I liked it. No matter where you sit you get an OK view which is nice and uncommon. If you're a Wynn or Encore hotel guest you can get tickets at $99 which are listed at $125, so that's a good deal and helpful. What I saw as an individual show was a few really good feats of athleticism. The acrobat's, the acrobatics, the aerialists, the performers are good in there, are just really really good. But a lot of it I can say in some shows of Cirque du Soleil, I've seen feats just as great. It's the story that really let it down or the story didn't exist or wasn't very good and I left not really knowing what was going on. The biggest problem is the story's really bad or unclear, weak or doesn't exist at all. There's just too much going on at the same time. Too many things moving. Too many visuals and too many "oh cool, amazing" stuff. A show with less going on might be better. The individual feats were really strong, and it was good as a show, but I was not too impressed and my company of friends and me did not feel impressed. And a couple of my friends did enjoy it. But for myself, I'd say if you haven't gone see it if possible, maybe check it out and if you're a Wynn guest, it's a good deal. Would see again or pay for this again? Probably not. It's trying to be a big spectacular flashy Vegas show, more means better? More just means too much and more chaotic.

Bring one broken household item. Walk up to the desk when you arrive, get your number. That number is your place in the line, so hold onto the paper, don't lose it or someone will take it. The pros are all volunteers, first come first served. When its your number and your turn call you're next in line, but go grab your stuff before the volunteers go home at 4:00 PM. They dont store stuff overnight. Make sure you are able to stay to get the item, otherwise you'll spend the whole day waiting and then it won't work. We can't help them all. Just cooperate, keep calm so it doesn't make everyone's day a pain.

A flotevalve controls filling trough with the float connected to a valve. When water goes down it goes down and opens the valve and water comes in. water rises it rises and start to close gradually. At the set level the valve should go shut and it stops. two normal things that cause overflow, one, a debris or mineral stuff is stuck or whatever on top of the valve that prevents it from closing completely. And also if you adjust the flote to high it will go over the level line already and after that it will close.

To all Enron employees,

these are difficult times we know. with the problems we face inside Enron and the worrying events happening around us, I just think this holiday season feels really strange for being a holiday. there was a lot of conversation about the all Enron holiday party scheduled for Dec 8th. folks felt really different. some thought it's going to be a great opportunity for us to get together and celebrate. others thought its not really appropriate now. i get why people feel it is, or isn't. it all makes sense.
given everything that happened in the past month we've gone ahead with canceling the party. i don't think its really appropriate to spend company money to celebrate now and we're taking the risk of looking imprudent.
sorry guys. you guys have been working hard. it's time we recognized your outstanding contributions, and I feel we need to celebrate now. but the holidays aren't the right time to celebrate with the party. i hope we can find other, more appropriate ways for us to celebrate all year, but we will definitely find a good way to celebrate this holiday season as well.
Ken Lay

So a siphon moves water from one container to another using gravity or the atmospheric pressure, to help move the water over a bump or some kind of hump. It just works. And to get it going you start with the tube filled entirely with water, so there is this continuous column. And what then happens is that the longer leg of the tube, which is sort of on the way down, gravity just pulls water down it, to the lower container. And as it's pulled downwards, what you get is a partial vacuum or lower pressure on the top bit. And because you've got this little vacuum, the atmospheric pressure on the water in the source container forces more water up the short leg to fill the air. Then you get this pressure differential that causes the water to continue. So this continues for as long as the exit is lower than the surface. The source has to be lower. If you get it the other way around, or if it's the same level, it won't work, because you need gravity doing the work. You need the lower leg to be heavier than the upper leg. If the water's not lower, gravity can't pull enough force to lift it up. So it's really just that weight or force that makes water move. And what also stops it is, if air gets in there, it breaks that column of water that's been going. And if there are air bubbles in there, it stops the whole process of the water being able to suck. Because it's air now in the tube. So the pressure inside is same as the air outside. It's not creating that differential to force more water up. So then you need to do all that priming, filling the tube with water again.

A piece of it. A yellow legal pad paper was poking out of a book in a plastic bag.

A book always ends up there on Thursdays, on the top of my flour sifter bin. And it's always the Count of Mont Cristo. With the Richmond Public Library stamp on the cover.

I can't see how they get in. It's squeaky screen door, I should hear it. But at 3 AM I'm mostly yeast and caffeine. Brain isn't working well anyway.

Tonight though, a piece of paper was poking out like a bookmark. So I wiped hands on apron, just a ghosty smudge of white on the dark apron cloth. Pulled the note out: page 142. Please, i think they're watching the drop box now. Spiky writing, really frantic.

A little weather just rushed in, smelled like wet tarmac, rain coming through the kitchen.

I looked out into the dark windows front of house. Just my own reflection staring back.

Decided not to open the book. And carefully stuck it back in between the pages. Put it in a brown pastry bag, and folded over twice to seal it.

Bought this one second hand and paid £38 for it. So far i have got roughly £38 worth of keyboard, perhaps a bit more
Flaws, start with the obvious. space bar rattles, does not simply click, but clatters like a bunch of cutlery in a tray every time I type, not a gentle sound, just a clatter. I have stopped noticing through the day, but late at night it becomes much louder than has any right to be. There is another flaw. The E key occasionally repeats itself, so meeting comes out like meeeting. It happens maybe once in every few paragraphs, often enough to leave me proofreading.
Contacting the seller was really slow. Before buying I asked what switches it had, he sent me a reply a week after I bought it and the keyboard had arrived at my place. It had brown switches, for the record.
Now for the surprising bits, genuinely comfy to type. Keys are cushioned, and I can write long emails and my wrists don't complain or anything. Not sure how I got away with my old laptop and its flat keyboard.
I have considered sending it back, but it doesn't seem worth the hassle. So it stays on my desk. Rattles, repeats, but earns its keep.
Three stars

Old school attendance registers help historians reconstruct patterns of daily life that are often missing from official narratives. For instance, you see who came to school on any particular day; did the student come or not. But not just if they came but why, or if they came. And then, as historians can use it to, say, guess what the season was or the needs of the village and labor and so on. Or the illness. Or bad weather that might have kept students or not. Or poverty, or family, or migration, or any sort of local emergency. You can also see if there are differences by gender, age, by the neighborhood where they live or by different social classes, and understand how school fitted into work and household routines and general community expectations. When you look over many, many years, you can even see changes in schooling habits and changes in public health. The problem is that attendance registers only record what the school chose to note. So, you never really know what the kids experienced, their experience in detail, or maybe you don't know for sure if the teachers reported absences correctly or that they're incomplete or it's just the teacher's assumptions. But that's not really a problem. I wouldn't say it's not really a problem. But, they're really, really only useful when you compare them to something else, a newspaper or a census. Something else, other information.

So every Thursday at 2:17 in the morning there’d be this library book in the back step of the bakery. Same book always. Its a field guide to north american moths, had a county library sticker on the spine and it was ghost pale. A little flour worked into the jacket as if the book itself had been helping at times. She did return it twice. The librarians smiled too politely I guess. At the third week she kept the book beside her rye starter and said nothing. And tonight rain was ticking off the alley door, ovens breathing. Mara was forming croissants pressing butter into the dough, and her palms were pressed against it, when the latch made this small and almost guilty click. No one there. Just this book on the wet concrete, as dry as a bone. She wiped her hands on her apron and she opened it. And there was a slip of paper in between “Luna Moth” and “Promethea” folded just once. The note said your window is the only light on this street, I read here until the first bus, and im sorry about the crumbs. Mara looked at the alley the dented milk crates, steam rising off the drains. The city felt large and then its not. And she tore a corner of an order pad and wrote “Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05.” And she put the note in the book. Then set it on a warm windowsill, opened back door and unlocked it.

so basically this class project, they wanted to compare some folded cardboard bridges. so they made several designs short beam, and then arch-inspire designs, and then triangular folds. They all had the same cardboard, so it was as consistent as we can get it all the same length same width or something, same cardboard. And they placed them between two supports, so they had it in here, they had them placed and they put weights on them so they'd break. And this is limited because it's handmade construction, so it won't be the exact same bridge every time. And only a limited number of trials and classroom conditions. So, so its not a real engineering data. But, overall it does say that triangular folds, they were more steady in holding the weight in this experiment in this activity. So, it does show how geometry, the fold geometry, does have an effect on the stability of the bridges.

Marguerite found the book lying open on the steel table by the back door, right under the bench where the bread peels hang. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*. The Harbor Street branch stamp on the cover had a due date in March. They nailed the mail slot in that door shut years ago, and the hatch they use for the flour man's deliveries never latched properly.

Eleven thursdays. She asked the day staff, checked the hatch for scratches from books sliding into the mail slot, even once staying past four with her coat on. Nothing. So then book always comes sometime between two and four and Marguerite is at the ovens and her back's to the door when it shows up.

Tonight a receipt from a grocery store, Pell's I think, is folded into the oystercatcher pages. The pencil's gone blotchy and messy, someone writing with too hard pressure at least once.

I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want.

She was still salty, was it or salt was her. Pages smelled salty. She got pencil out of her apron pocket and on the receipt wrote bring it on Thursday I'll have a roll. Tucked it back into the oystercatcher and put book on the hatch side ledge. In paper bag put warm roll right next to it.

I live in Toronto now so no Hydra Ottawa or any other local utility bills. But I'm writing this for the rest of the people who deal with it, it's just alarming how they bill people. So I had an account for a year, was renting a place downtown. So I moved back in with my parents. I was going to do an MA so I cancelled the account, paid all bills that I owed. But then what happened is I was still getting billed. They would dip money out of my account at random intervals that I was not even informed about. Over a year, my account was still being charged despite I had officially cancelled the account. I called. I sent all proof that was being paid from my bank account and still they kept telling me that my account was closed, that no charges are being charged. And my parents and I sat down one day and went through the bills and realized this wasn't my bank account. It turned out, so because I had told them I was moving in with my parents and my dad's phone number or ID number for utilities was the billing number, they had mistakenly linked me to the billing number. Then they were siphoning money from my bank account and crediting my dad's account. It wasn't caught for over a year. We caught it when we reviewed the bills together. It wasn't caught before that because my parents were constantly getting overpayment refunds. It was just normal to them. We then, it took hours on the phone to get them to fix it. We spoke to multiple representatives. A manager came in, looked at it and apologized, fixed it. Refused to give any refund and offered an apology. That's ridiculous. Going forward I will never give them my banking details to have automatic bills paid. The way that they handle your data, you've all got to be really concerned.

so it's like 3:40am, second batch of rye is in proof. Marisol spots it again—this "field guide to night birds" from the library, just on the flour bin by the back door, still cold from hanging around in the alley. And for four four Thursdays in a row now, and it's the same book. Stamped Eastgate branch, three weeks out past due. Every single time she'd take it to the book drop box on her way home. And Thursday it was back, like the building borrowed it. She dries her hands on her apron and flips it open. Pulls out a index card folded. It's got her name "R" on the other side. So she leaves her vent fans going, the alley is smelly like bread and it just won't get it past five o'clock. She walks her mom's dog every day. Her mom can't and she keeps on forgetting that she returns this, and she thinks maybe she just doesn't want to. And then she reads it for the second time while she waits for the timer to go off. Outside fan keeps humming, pushing warm air into the dark. And she turns over her card again, writes "Ry is coming out at 4.15" her grease pencil, then takes a piece of heel from yesterday's loaf and she puts some of wax paper around it, on top on the book, opens up the back door just an inch, and leaves there for this R person to take the book and the piece of bread.

So this one is actually really common. The weather did that last week on me. So Tuesday, it rained for days and by Thursday half of my branywines had split. Just right down the side, this split is the seam of the fruit. So when you have a dry spell followed by a deluge or a torrential rain. Because there's not a ton of sun. And in a few hours, there's no sun and no light. And the inside of the fruit takes in water faster than the skin can hold and it's got to hold on. So if you see a lot of splits in branywine, this is the issue. So far, my sun golds, not too many splits. But I do have a few that are looking like they might follow. And that is the same story, weather. So you can't really get out of it. Once it's happened. But all I could do is keep that two-day picking schedule on more of an even keel. But it's not going to make any difference. I just think the rest of the rest of the plants and the vine are going to give me a good crop anyway, right? I just pick the split fruit and it's just going to be used for something else. Now that this is going to continue to be more of an issue for branywines. So this is the problem is that branywine, because of its thick skin, is going to split. I think for sun-gold I would have luck if you do less water in a one go.

Thursdays a book shows up in the bread shop. It's not on the counter mind you, it gets wedged behind the flour bins by the back door like whoever leaves it knows I won't trip over it. Its the same one always "A Field Guide to North American Moths" Elmwood branch due date stamped so long ago that the ink has gone violet. I've never seen anyone drop it off, I'm elbow deep in rye dough by two o'clock, and honestly at that time of day I wouldn't notice a marching band. First few weeks I put it on the shelf by the register, and it would be gone Friday morning, then here Thursday again, whatever, people are strange, and I talk to my sourdough starter so I'll stop judgment. But tonight, on page 114 about the luna moth there's a note tucked in. Pencil, but pressed hard. The note reads, they only live for a week, they don't even eat. I think what a waste a beautiful thing, do you get to see the bread before it's gone? No signature just a note. Read it twice then a third time while the ovens tick away, then pulled the first loaf of the night still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper and put it behind the flour bins.

You can get hot in there, or the humidity is high so it'll feel pretty muggy. If its too humid, the air will feel stuffy. Low airflow and poor ventilation can be a problem. Your body releases heat, and your breath releases CO2 and smells etc. Air will feel stale. I think what I've had a problem on my house, that in a hot climate, you can cool down the room and the humidity stays high and the air is still pretty muggy. But the air has to move and air conditioning will keep you comfortable, but you need to open the window or use a fan or ventilation system to make it feel fresher in there and bring down the moisture that makes it feel heavy and stale in there.

I was always told you work from home is a win for everyone. It really isn't. Been mentoring junior engineers for the last couple of years. And what they require isn't tickets and doc and a set schedule meetings. They are trying to actually participate in design conversation, watching somebody else figure out a pesky bug, getting answers while uncertainty is still small before it starts turning into something that is way larger. And you get it all, free, when in office. Work from home they must figure out when to intrude, get calls set up, and explain a problem they likely don't know it well enough. And this is really something hard to ask of someone who has not yet had a chance to learn these.

I've seen this model really damage how well you can get feedback. A short comment for code review starts being read as absolute verdict. And delay on getting responses, it is a killer of forward movement. I was working with these people, they were able to progress much more quickly when they could sit next to senior and pair, work things out on whiteboard, and actually touch a senior in person.

This is not saying we should remove flexibility. It works if you can drive your own work. For junior, it is being together with others that gets them to the desired skill level, to pick up on confidence and context and judgment they need. You end up really bad technical leadership in the future, if you start handing over a laptop to the newbie with a calendar and that is it.

A rain gauge is simple. It's just some water collected in a known area and what you get is depth in millimeters or inches. So if no draining happens, this is how much water on a plain surface with no draining or evaporation or absorption. They typically have a funnel. It's wide opening and then it feeds into a thin measuring tube, the same quantity of water would go higher and then the tube scale is adjusted for the area ratio to get to the actual rain depth. But there's a big issue of wind error because wind carries droplets. So if it's blustery, raindrops will go over the opening, and you might get under counting. Sometimes evaporation before reading, or just rain splashing into the tube also distorts it.

Old school attendance registers are a massive source of information for people doing history of local life in past communities. If you just look at who did or didn't show up at school you can work out what was going on. Seasons matter: bad weather in winter, harvest season, and flu epidemics. And of course they can reveal other stuff as well: for a particular group being persistently absent you can infer some kind of social and cultural difference. But the problem is that sometimes data is fudged by admin staff or heads of schools, either intentionally or due to just lack of care, because they had to get grants. So the data isn't necessarily an accurate reflection of attendance. Also, they tend not to show reasons why people are absent. So for researchers it is very important, very critical to cross-referencing with outside evidence to see what was actually happening in the community, or other community evidence. For example if you want to understand the social structure or something, then you need to see other evidence, other information to support your conclusions.

Most people think the floats are going to work, but it doesn't matter what they're made of. If it falls over into the water, or the washer is fouled with debris, then the valve doesn't close all the way. If it doesn't seal, obviously you're going to have an issue. That's the majority of problems people have. Or it gets a leak hole in it so it takes on water. And the ball is too heavy for this little mechanism to hold it up.
